lesson.hook: In 1851 the French physicist Léon Foucault hung a 28-kilogram metal ball on a wire 67 meters long from the dome of the Panthéon, a huge stone building in Paris, and set it swinging. A swinging weight like this, a **pendulum**, keeps swinging back and forth along the same line unless something pushes it sideways. Nothing pushed Foucault’s pendulum. Yet as visitors watched, the line of its swing crept slowly around the floor, about 11 degrees every hour. The pendulum was holding its line. The floor, the building, the city and all the ground under Paris were turning beneath it. You are turning right now, too. That turning, together with two other motions of Earth and the Moon, explains most of what you will see the first time you really look up.
lesson.overview: This chapter starts where every astronomer starts: outside, looking up, with nothing but your eyes. Section 1.1 explains why the Sun, Moon and stars rise and set, and how Foucault showed that it is the ground, not the sky, that turns. Section 1.2 explains why the Moon changes shape over a month. Section 1.3 explains summer and winter and clears away the most common wrong explanation. Along the way you meet the two tools used in every later chapter: the pocket scale model, in which the Sun is a ball about 20 cm (8 inches) across and Earth is a peppercorn, and your sky diary, which you start at the end of this chapter. In Chapter 2 the scale model grows outward to hold all the planets.
objectives: Explain why the Sun, Moon and stars rise in the east and set in the west, using Earth’s rotation.
Predict the Moon’s phase, and the time of day it is up, from where it sits relative to the Sun.
Explain how Earth’s 23.4-degree tilt, not its distance from the Sun, causes the seasons.
Describe the observations behind each explanation: Foucault’s pendulum, the daytime Moon, and opposite seasons in the two hemispheres.
Start a sky diary that records the Moon’s shape and position and one bright planet.

sections.title: Day, night and the spinning Earth
reading: Watch the sky for a day and a night and you will see a pattern. The Sun comes up in the east, climbs across the sky and goes down in the west. After dark the stars do the same, and so does the Moon. For thousands of years most people assumed that the sky was turning around a motionless Earth. In fact Earth spins like a top around an **axis**, an imaginary line through the North Pole, the center of the planet and the South Pole. One full turn is called a **rotation**. Measured against the distant stars, one rotation takes 23 hours 56 minutes, a **sidereal day**. Measured from one noon to the next, the day we set our clocks by, it takes 24 hours, a **solar day**. The extra four minutes come from Earth’s yearly trip around the Sun, which you will meet in Section 1.3 [1, 2].

At any moment the Sun lights one half of Earth. On that half it is day, and on the other half it is night. Earth turns from west to east, so each morning it carries you out of the dark half and into the light. That moment is sunrise. In the evening it carries you back into the dark half, and that is sunset (Figure 1.1). Because the ground under you is moving toward the east, everything in the sky seems to slide the other way, toward the west, the way trees seem to slide backward past the window of a moving train. Earth turns fast. A point on the equator travels about 1,670 km (1,040 miles) every hour, faster than a jet airliner flies [2]. You do not feel it because the motion is smooth and steady, just as you cannot feel a smooth flight with your eyes closed.

Earth turns a full circle, 360 degrees, in about 24 hours, so the sky seems to turn 15 degrees every hour. You can measure angles on the sky with your own hand: held out at arm’s length, your closed fist covers about 10 degrees. Not everything in the sky moves the same amount. Earth’s axis points at a spot in the northern sky called the **north celestial pole**, and the stars seem to wheel around that spot once a day. A star of medium brightness, Polaris, the North Star, sits less than one degree from it, so Polaris hardly moves while all the other stars circle it [1]. From the Southern Hemisphere, Polaris is below the horizon, and no bright star marks the south pole of the sky.

For most of history nobody could tell by looking whether the sky or the ground was turning. Foucault’s pendulum settled the question. Nothing in a pendulum makes its swing turn by itself. If Earth stood still, the swing would stay lined up with the same marks on the floor all day. Instead, at the latitude of Paris, the line of the swing turns about 11 degrees an hour and goes all the way around in about 32 hours [3, 4]. That is what a spinning Earth predicts. At the North Pole the floor would turn a full circle under the pendulum in one rotation. At the equator it would not turn at all, and in between the rate depends on latitude. Foucault’s report was read to the French Academy of Sciences in February 1851, and within months copies of his pendulum were swinging in cities around the world [3, 4].

To keep sizes and distances straight, this book uses one scale model all the way through, based on Guy Ottewell’s Thousand-Yard Model. In it, every 100,000 miles (about 160,000 km) of real space shrinks to one inch (2.5 cm) [5]. The Sun becomes a ball about 20 cm (8 inches) across, the size of a bowling ball. Earth becomes a peppercorn about 2 mm wide, sitting about 24 m (26 yards) from the ball, roughly the length of two school buses [5]. Picture that peppercorn spinning once a day while the bowling ball lights the half facing it. Every sunrise anyone has ever seen happened on that turning speck. Keep the peppercorn in mind. In the next section we add the Moon beside it, and in Chapter 2 we walk out to the other planets.

example.title: Worked example: where will the Moon be in two hours?
steps: At 7:00 p.m. you see the Moon low in the east, about one fist above the horizon. You want to know where it will be at 9:00 p.m.
Earth turns 360 degrees in about 24 hours, so the sky seems to turn 360 ÷ 24 = 15 degrees per hour.
In 2 hours the sky turns 2 × 15 = 30 degrees. One fist at arm’s length covers about 10 degrees, so the Moon will move about three fists.

Objects rising in the east climb along a slanting path. From the Northern Hemisphere it slants up and to the right, toward the south, so the Moon gains only about two fists of height. Expect it roughly three fists above the horizon and somewhat to the right of where you first saw it.
The Moon also drifts slowly east against the stars (Section 1.2), but only about its own width per hour, which is tiny next to 30 degrees.
example.takeaway: The whole sky turns about 15 degrees an hour, one and a half fists, so you can predict where anything in the sky will be a few hours from now.

misconception.myth: The Sun moves across the sky from east to west, so it must be going around us every day.
misconception.fact: The Sun’s daily trip across the sky is caused by Earth turning from west to east once a day, which carries us past the Sun the way a train carries you past a tree. Foucault’s pendulum shows that the ground itself is turning. Earth does travel around the Sun, but that takes a year, not a day (Section 1.3).

practice.q: Why do the stars rise in the east and set in the west?
choices: The stars travel around Earth once a day
Earth spins from west to east once a day
Earth goes around the Sun once a day
The Moon pulls the stars across the sky
practice.explanation: Earth’s west-to-east spin makes everything in the sky appear to move from east to west. The stars do not circle Earth, and Earth takes a year, not a day, to go around the Sun.

practice.q: A Foucault pendulum is set up exactly on the equator, in Ecuador. What happens to the line of its swing during one day?
choices: It turns a full circle in 24 hours
It turns a full circle in about 32 hours
It does not turn at all
It turns twice as fast as in Paris
practice.explanation: At the equator the floor is carried around Earth’s axis but does not twist around under the pendulum, so the swing stays on the same line. At the poles it turns a full circle in one rotation, and Paris, in between, takes about 32 hours.

practice.q: Imagine standing exactly at the North Pole on a long winter night. Describe how the stars move during the night, and explain why.
practice.answer: Polaris would be almost straight overhead, because Earth’s axis comes up through your feet and points at the north celestial pole. Every other star would circle around Polaris, moving parallel to the horizon at 15 degrees an hour. No star would rise or set; the same stars would stay up all night, just going around.
practice.explanation: A good answer puts Polaris (the north celestial pole) overhead, says the stars circle it parallel to the horizon without rising or setting, and ties this to Earth spinning around an axis that points straight up at the pole.

sections.title: The Moon and its phases
reading: The Moon is the nearest world to us and the easiest to watch. It is a ball of rock about 3,475 km across, a little more than a quarter as wide as Earth, and it circles Earth at an average distance of about 384,400 km [1, 2]. Light crosses that gap in about 1.3 seconds. The Moon makes no light of its own; its glow is sunlight bouncing off its gray, dusty surface [1]. Add it to the pocket scale model and it becomes a speck about half a millimeter wide, like a grain of sand, circling the peppercorn Earth only about 6 cm (2.4 inches) away [3]. The bowling-ball Sun is still 24 m off. So at any moment, sunlight reaches the Moon and Earth from almost exactly the same direction.

The Sun always lights half of the Moon, the half that faces the Sun. What changes over a month is how much of that lit half is turned toward us [4]. The Moon travels around Earth along a path called an **orbit**, and the shape of the lit part we see from Earth is called the Moon’s **phase**. When the Moon is roughly between Earth and the Sun, its lit half faces away from us and we see nothing: this is the **new Moon**. Then a thin sliver of the lit half comes into view, a **crescent**. About a week after new Moon we see half of the Moon’s face lit. This is a **first quarter** Moon, because the Moon is a quarter of the way around its orbit. Next comes a **gibbous** Moon, more than half lit, and about two weeks after new Moon, with the Moon on the far side of Earth from the Sun, we see the whole lit half: a **full Moon** (Figure 1.2).

After full Moon the same shapes return in reverse order: waning gibbous, third quarter (also called last quarter), waning crescent, and new Moon again. **Waxing** means growing and **waning** means shrinking. One full cycle of phases, from new Moon to the next new Moon, takes about 29.5 days, the **lunar month** [1, 4]. Measured against the stars, the Moon actually goes once around Earth in about 27.3 days. It needs about two days more to get back to new Moon because Earth has moved along its own path around the Sun in the meantime, so the Moon must travel a little farther to line up with the Sun again [1, 2].

The phase also tells you when to look. Each day the Moon moves about 12 degrees farther east of the Sun, so it rises later each day, on average about 50 minutes later, though the exact delay varies [1]. A full Moon sits opposite the Sun, so it rises around sunset, sets around sunrise and is up all night. A first quarter Moon is highest in the sky around sunset and sets around midnight. A third quarter Moon rises around midnight and is still up through the morning. A young waxing crescent hangs low in the west just after sunset. So for much of the month you can find the Moon in the daytime sky. From the Northern Hemisphere a waxing Moon is lit on its right side. From Australia or Argentina the view is flipped, and a waxing Moon is lit on its left.

A daytime Moon shows that Earth’s shadow is not the cause of the phases. On a clear afternoon about a week after new Moon, you can see a half-lit Moon and the Sun in the sky at the same time, and the Moon’s lit side always points toward the Sun. Earth’s shadow points away from the Sun, so it cannot be falling on a Moon that sits off to one side of the Sun. Earth’s shadow does sometimes reach the Moon, but only at full Moon, when the Sun, Earth and Moon line up. That event is a **lunar eclipse**. It does not happen every month because the Moon’s orbit is tilted by about 5 degrees, so the full Moon usually passes just above or below the shadow [1, 2]. One more pattern: the Moon spins once for each trip around Earth, so the same face always points toward us. The far side is not dark; it is in full sunlight at new Moon [1].

keyTerms.def: The path one object follows around another, such as the Moon around Earth or Earth around the Sun.
The shape of the sunlit part of the Moon as seen from Earth on a given day.
Waxing means the lit part we see is growing (new to full); waning means it is shrinking (full to new).
A crescent Moon shows less than half its face lit; a gibbous Moon shows more than half but not all.
The time from one new Moon to the next, about 29.5 days.

example.title: Worked example: the lamp-and-ball Moon
steps: In a dark room, put a lamp with its shade removed at one end, at about head height. Hold a ball (an orange works) at arm’s length. Your head is Earth, the ball is the Moon and the lamp is the Sun.
Face the lamp with the ball held just above it. The side of the ball facing you is dark: new Moon.

Turn slowly to your left, keeping the ball in front of your face. This is the direction the Moon moves for Northern Hemisphere viewers. After an eighth of a turn a thin crescent lit on the right appears; after a quarter turn the right half is lit: first quarter.

Keep turning until your back is to the lamp, holding the ball a little above the shadow of your head. The whole face you see is lit: full Moon. Keep going and you see the left half lit (third quarter), then a thin crescent lit on the left.

Notice that the lamp lit exactly half of the ball the whole time. Only the angle you viewed it from changed, and your head’s shadow never touched the ball except when you let it at full Moon, which is the model’s lunar eclipse.
example.takeaway: The Moon’s phase depends only on the angle between the Sun, the Moon and you; no shadow is involved.

misconception.myth: The Moon changes shape because Earth’s shadow covers part of it.
misconception.fact: Phases come from seeing more or less of the Moon’s sunlit half as it goes around Earth. Earth’s shadow points away from the Sun, so it can only reach a full Moon, and then only during a lunar eclipse. A crescent Moon is seen close to the Sun in the sky, where Earth’s shadow could never fall on it.

practice.q: You see a full Moon rising in the east. Where is the Sun?
choices: Setting in the west, or just below the western horizon
Rising in the east right behind the Moon
Directly between Earth and the Moon
practice.explanation: A full Moon is opposite the Sun in the sky, so when it rises in the east the Sun is setting in the west. If the Sun were between Earth and the Moon we would see a new Moon, not a full one.

practice.q: You are in the Northern Hemisphere. At sunset you see the Moon high in the southern sky with its right half lit. Which phase is it?
practice.explanation: A first quarter Moon is 90 degrees east of the Sun, so it is highest around sunset, and from the Northern Hemisphere its right half is lit. A waxing crescent would be low in the west, a full Moon would be rising in the east, and a third quarter Moon is lit on the left and rises around midnight.

practice.q: A classmate says, “Tonight’s thin crescent Moon is mostly in Earth’s shadow.” Using where the crescent appears in the sky, explain why this cannot be right.
practice.answer: A thin crescent is always seen close to the Sun in the sky, low in the west after sunset or low in the east before dawn. That means the Moon is nearly between Earth and the Sun. Earth’s shadow points directly away from the Sun, so it cannot fall on a Moon in that direction. We see a crescent because most of the Moon’s sunlit half faces away from us and only its edge is turned toward Earth.
practice.explanation: A good answer places the crescent near the Sun in the sky, notes that Earth’s shadow points away from the Sun, and explains the shape by our viewing angle on the sunlit half.

sections.title: Seasons
reading: Ask people why summer is warm and many will say that Earth is closer to the Sun then. It sounds sensible, because a campfire feels hotter when you step closer. The numbers say otherwise. Earth’s path around the Sun is very nearly a circle. Its distance ranges from about 147.1 million km at the closest point, called **perihelion**, to about 152.1 million km at the farthest, called **aphelion**, a difference of only about 3 percent [1]. And Earth reaches perihelion in early January, in the middle of the northern winter [2]. In the pocket scale model the peppercorn sits about 24 m from the bowling ball, and over a whole year that distance changes by less than one meter, about one long step [3].

A second clue settles it. Seasons are opposite in the two halves of the planet. In December, while people in Canada shovel snow, people in Australia and Argentina go to the beach. If distance caused the seasons, the whole Earth would have summer at the same time [2]. The real cause is a tilt. Earth’s axis is not straight up and down compared with its path around the Sun; it leans by about 23.4 degrees, Earth’s **axial tilt** [1]. The axis also keeps pointing the same way in space all year, toward Polaris. So around June 21 the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun, and around December 21 it leans away (Figure 1.3). These two dates are the **solstices**. Halfway between, around March 20 and September 22, neither hemisphere leans toward the Sun. These are the **equinoxes**, when day and night are close to 12 hours each almost everywhere on Earth [2].

Leaning toward the Sun matters in two ways. First, the Sun climbs higher in the sky, and sunlight from high up is more concentrated. Shine a flashlight straight down at a table and you get a small, bright circle. Tilt the flashlight and the same light spreads into a bigger, dimmer oval. Low winter sunlight is like the tilted flashlight: the same sunshine is spread over more ground, so each square meter gets less. Second, the days are longer, and more hours of sunshine with fewer hours of night means more heating [2]. At 40 degrees north, the latitude of Philadelphia, Madrid and Beijing, the noon Sun stands about 73 degrees above the horizon at the June solstice but only about 27 degrees at the December solstice. The day lasts roughly 15 hours in June and roughly 9 hours in December.

The same tilt explains the most extreme places on Earth. At and north of the **Arctic Circle**, about 66.6 degrees north, the Sun stays up for 24 hours around the June solstice, the midnight Sun, and does not rise at all around the December solstice. The number 66.6 is simply 90 minus the tilt. Between about 23.4 degrees north and 23.4 degrees south, in the tropics, the Sun passes straight overhead at noon on at least one day a year, and temperatures change less through the year. If Earth had no tilt at all, every place would get close to 12 hours of daylight every day of the year, and there would be almost no seasons [2].

Distance does have a small effect. Because sunlight spreads out as it travels, Earth receives about 7 percent more sunlight in early January than in early July [1]. That is real, but it is outweighed by the tilt, which shifts the noon Sun at any mid-northern latitude by about 47 degrees between June and December. You can watch this shift without any equipment. Stand a stick upright in the ground and mark the tip of its shadow at midday once a month. North of the tropics, the noon shadow is shortest around the June solstice and longest around the December solstice. People have kept this kind of record with upright posts called **gnomons** since ancient times.

Now it is your turn to look up. Starting tonight, keep a **sky diary**: a notebook or phone note with one short entry for each clear night you look. Write the date, the time, where you stood and what you saw. Sketch the Moon’s shape, note which side is lit, and record where it sits: its compass direction and how many fists it is above the horizon. Then look for a planet. The five planets that are easy to see with your eyes alone, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn, all stay close to the **ecliptic**, the line across the sky that the Sun follows through the year, and they usually shine with a steadier light than the twinkling stars [2]. Venus, when it is up, is the brightest object in the night sky after the Moon. With binoculars held steady, Jupiter shows up to four of its moons as tiny dots beside it.

example.title: Worked example: how much stronger is June sunlight at 40 degrees north?
steps: Find where the Sun is overhead. At the June solstice the noon Sun is straight overhead at 23.4 degrees north; at the December solstice it is overhead at 23.4 degrees south.
Noon height of the Sun = 90 degrees minus the gap between your latitude and the latitude where the Sun is overhead. June: 90 − (40 − 23.4) = 73.4 degrees. December: 90 − (40 + 23.4) = 26.6 degrees.
Picture a beam of sunlight 1 meter wide. Arriving at 73 degrees, it spreads over about 1.04 meters of flat ground. Arriving at 27 degrees, it spreads over about 2.2 meters.

So at noon each square meter of ground gets about twice as much sunlight in June as in December (2.2 ÷ 1.04 is about 2.1). Add about 15 hours of daylight in June against about 9 in December, and summer wins easily.
Compare the distance effect: only about 7 percent, and in early January it actually favors the northern winter.
example.takeaway: The tilt changes how steeply sunlight arrives and how long it shines, and those two effects, not distance, make summer and winter.

misconception.myth: It’s summer because Earth is closer to the Sun.
misconception.fact: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, during the northern winter, and its distance changes by only about 3 percent over the year. The seasons are also opposite in the two hemispheres, which distance cannot explain. The 23.4-degree tilt of Earth’s axis changes how high the Sun climbs and how long the days last, and that is what makes the seasons.

practice.q: When is Earth closest to the Sun?
practice.explanation: Perihelion falls in early January, in the northern winter. Early July is aphelion, the farthest point. The solstices and equinoxes are set by the tilt, not by distance.

practice.q: Sydney, Australia, is at about 34 degrees south. Find the height of the noon Sun in Sydney at the December solstice, and say which season Sydney is having.
practice.answer: At the December solstice the noon Sun is overhead at 23.4 degrees south. The gap between Sydney’s latitude and that latitude is 34 − 23.4 = 10.6 degrees, so the noon Sun is 90 − 10.6, about 79 degrees high. The Sun is high and the days are long, so it is summer in Sydney.
practice.explanation: A good answer uses the Sun’s overhead latitude in December (23.4 degrees south), computes about 79 degrees, and connects a high noon Sun to summer in the Southern Hemisphere.

practice.q: Suppose Earth’s axis had no tilt at all. What would happen?
choices: Every place would have about 12 hours of daylight all year, and seasons would almost disappear
Only the equator would have 12-hour days
The Moon would stop showing phases
practice.explanation: With no tilt, neither hemisphere would ever lean toward the Sun, so the noon Sun’s height and the length of the day would stay the same all year everywhere. Only the small 3 percent distance change would remain. The Moon’s phases do not depend on Earth’s tilt.

interactives.intro: A photographer at about 40 degrees north, in Colorado, points a camera at Polaris on a dark, moonless night and leaves the shutter open for 4 hours. Think about each question before you reveal the answer.

steps.q: What shape will the star trails make in the photo?
steps.a: Arcs of circles, all centered on a point very close to Polaris, the north celestial pole. Polaris itself makes only a tiny arc, because it sits less than one degree from the pole. The arcs are Earth’s spin recorded on the picture.

steps.q: How much of a full circle will each arc cover?
steps.a: The sky turns about 15 degrees per hour, so in 4 hours each star moves through about 4 × 15 = 60 degrees, one sixth of a full circle.

steps.q: Next night the photographer points the camera due east instead. What do the trails look like now?
steps.a: Slanted lines climbing up from the horizon and to the right, toward the south. Stars rise at an angle in the east; at 40 degrees north the trails make an angle of about 50 degrees (90 minus the latitude) with the horizon.

steps.q: What would the eastern photo look like from the equator, in Ecuador?
steps.a: The trails would rise straight up from the horizon. At the equator the celestial poles sit on the northern and southern horizons, so stars rise vertically, and Polaris would be just at, or hidden by, the northern horizon.

interactives.title: Put the phases in order
interactives.intro: Starting just after a new Moon, put these phases in the order you would see them over the next month. Use Figure 1.2 if you get stuck.
steps: Waxing crescent
First quarter
Waxing gibbous
Full Moon
Waning gibbous
Third quarter
Waning crescent
interactives.explain: The lit part grows (waxes) from new Moon to full Moon in about two weeks, then shrinks (wanes) back to new Moon. After the waning crescent comes the next new Moon, about 29.5 days after the last. From the Northern Hemisphere the waxing phases are lit on the right and the waning phases on the left.

interactives.title: How high does the noon Sun climb?
interactives.intro: Set your latitude (negative numbers are south of the equator) and slide through the year. Watch how the noon Sun’s height and the strength of its light change, and compare the north with the south on the same date. The Sun’s position here uses a simple formula that is accurate to within about two degrees.

inputs.label: Day of the year (172 is about June 21, 355 is about December 21)

outputs.label: Latitude where the Sun is straight overhead at noon
Height of the noon Sun above the horizon (below zero means it does not rise that day)
Noon sunlight on flat ground, compared with the Sun straight overhead (ignoring the air)

interactives.takeaway: At 40 degrees north the noon Sun swings from about 73 degrees high in June to about 27 degrees in December, and the sunlight landing on each square meter at noon roughly halves. Distance from the Sun is not in the formula at all; the tilt alone produces the seasons.

interactives.title: True, or a myth?
interactives.intro: These claims come from the whole chapter. Sort each one, then read why.

items.text: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January.
items.why: Perihelion falls in early January, in the middle of the northern winter.

items.text: Summer happens because Earth is closer to the Sun.
items.why: Distance changes by only about 3 percent, and the hemispheres have opposite seasons. The 23.4-degree tilt causes the seasons.

items.text: When it is summer in Canada, it is winter in Argentina.
items.why: When the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun, the Southern Hemisphere leans away.

items.text: The Moon’s phases are caused by Earth’s shadow.
items.why: Phases come from our changing view of the Moon’s sunlit half. Earth’s shadow reaches the Moon only during a lunar eclipse.

items.text: The Sun always lights half of the Moon, except during a lunar eclipse.
items.why: Like any ball in sunlight, the Moon always has a lit half. Only how much of it faces us changes.

items.text: You can only see the Moon at night.
items.why: For much of the month the Moon is up during the day; a first quarter Moon, for example, rises around noon.

items.text: The stars rise and set because Earth spins.
items.why: Earth’s west-to-east rotation makes the whole sky seem to turn east to west, 15 degrees an hour.

items.text: Polaris is the brightest star in the night sky.
items.why: Polaris is only medium-bright. It matters because it sits less than one degree from the north celestial pole. Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky.

items.text: At the equinoxes, day and night are close to 12 hours each almost everywhere.
items.why: At the equinoxes neither hemisphere leans toward the Sun, so the lit half of Earth splits every latitude roughly in half.

interactives.title: Speed up the turning sky
interactives.intro: In real life you need a whole night to see the sky wheel around Polaris. In SpaceEngine you can squeeze that night into a minute and watch it happen.
interactives.setup: SpaceEngine open, standing anywhere in the starting view.

steps.do: Find Earth: press Shift+H until Earth is selected (it cycles between the Milky Way, the Sun and Earth), then press G to fly there.
steps.see: The camera flies to Earth and stops near it.

steps.do: Land on Earth's surface somewhere in the Northern Hemisphere, on the night side, using SpaceEngine's landing control, and turn the view so you face north.
steps.see: You stand on the ground with stars overhead and a horizon below.

steps.do: Press L a few times to speed up time. The time rate shows in the lower left of the screen.
steps.see: The stars start to move. Each one swings around a single point in the northern sky.

steps.do: Look for the still point. Polaris sits less than one degree from it.
steps.see: Polaris hardly moves while every other star circles around it.

steps.do: Turn to face east, then press K to slow time back down and \ (backslash) to return to real time.
steps.see: In the east, stars climb up from the horizon at a slant; at normal speed the motion is too slow to notice.

interactives.notice: Nothing in the sky is really turning. The ground under you is, from west to east, so the sky seems to turn the other way, about 15 degrees every hour, around the north celestial pole.

check.q: With time sped up, which star in the northern sky barely moved?
choices: The star lowest on the horizon
None; they all moved the same amount
check.why: Polaris sits less than one degree from the north celestial pole, the point Earth's axis aims at, so it barely moves while the other stars circle it.

interactives.title: A month of Moon phases from above
interactives.intro: From Earth you only ever see the Moon from one side. Flying above the Earth and Moon lets you see the whole setup at once: Sun, Earth and Moon, and which half of the Moon is lit.

steps.do: Press Shift+H until Earth is selected and press G to fly to it. Back the camera away until you can see the Moon too, then turn so you look down on both from above.
steps.see: Earth and the Moon both look like half-lit balls, lit on the side facing the Sun.

steps.do: Press L several times to speed up time.
steps.see: The Moon moves around Earth. Its sunlit half always stays on the side toward the Sun.

steps.do: Watch where the Moon is when it sits between Earth and the Sun.
steps.see: Its lit half faces away from Earth. From Earth this is a new Moon.

steps.do: Keep watching until the Moon is on the far side of Earth from the Sun.
steps.see: Its lit half now faces Earth. This is a full Moon.

steps.do: Watch the time readout as the Moon comes back to the new Moon position, then press \ (backslash) for real time.
steps.see: About 29.5 days have gone by in the date readout.

interactives.notice: Half of the Moon is always lit, the half facing the Sun. The phases are only how much of that lit half we can see from Earth as the Moon goes around us, one full cycle in about 29.5 days.

check.q: From above, the Moon sat on the far side of Earth from the Sun. What phase would someone on Earth see?
check.why: The lit half of the Moon faces the Sun, and from that spot it also faces Earth, so we see the whole lit face: a full Moon.

interactives.title: Noon Sun in June and December
interactives.intro: The seasons come from Earth's 23.4-degree tilt, not its distance from the Sun. In SpaceEngine you can stand in one spot and jump between the solstices to watch the noon Sun change height.

steps.do: Press Shift+H until Earth is selected, press G to fly there, and land on Earth's surface at a mid-northern spot, facing south.
steps.see: You stand on the ground with the southern horizon in front of you.

steps.do: Open the time settings and set the date to 21 June at local noon.
steps.see: The Sun stands high in the southern sky.

steps.do: Without moving, set the date to 21 December at local noon.
steps.see: The Sun sits much lower over the southern horizon.

steps.do: Press L to speed time through a full December day, then \ (backslash) for real time.
steps.see: The Sun makes a short, low arc, rising and setting well south of east and west.

interactives.notice: Same place, same clock time, and yet the noon Sun is far higher in June. Earth's tilt aims the Northern Hemisphere toward the Sun in June and away from it in December, so sunlight comes in steeper and days last longer in summer.

check.q: In the Northern Hemisphere, when was the noon Sun higher in the sky?
check.why: In June the northern half of Earth is tilted toward the Sun, so the noon Sun stands higher and its light falls more directly.

quiz.q: How long is one solar day, from one noon to the next?
quiz.explanation: A solar day is 24 hours. Earth’s spin measured against the stars, the sidereal day, is about 4 minutes shorter. 27.3 days is the Moon’s orbit against the stars, and 365 days is a year.

quiz.q: A bright star is due south at 10 p.m. About how far west will it have moved by 1 a.m.?
quiz.explanation: The sky turns about 15 degrees per hour. From 10 p.m. to 1 a.m. is 3 hours, so 3 × 15 = 45 degrees, about four and a half fists.

quiz.q: Why does Polaris barely move across the sky during the night?
choices: It lies very close to the point in the sky that Earth’s axis points to
It is the closest star to Earth
It is the brightest star in the sky
It circles Earth once a day
quiz.explanation: Polaris is less than one degree from the north celestial pole, the pivot the sky seems to turn around. It is neither the closest nor the brightest star.

choices: Earth’s shadow falling on part of the Moon
The Moon’s distance from Earth changing
Seeing different amounts of the Moon’s sunlit half as it orbits Earth
quiz.explanation: The Sun always lights half of the Moon, and our view of that half changes as the Moon goes around Earth. Earth’s shadow reaches the Moon only during a lunar eclipse, and the Moon has no clouds.

quiz.q: Tonight the Moon is full. About what will it look like one week from now?
quiz.explanation: A quarter of the 29.5-day cycle is about a week. After full Moon the next quarter phase is third quarter. First quarter and waxing crescent come before full Moon.

quiz.q: At 8 a.m. you see the Moon fairly high in the southern sky with its left half lit. You are in the Northern Hemisphere. Which phase is it?
quiz.explanation: A third quarter Moon rises around midnight and is highest around sunrise, so it is still well up in the morning, and from the Northern Hemisphere its left half is lit. A first quarter Moon is lit on the right and is up in the afternoon and evening.

choices: at its closest to the Sun
at its farthest from the Sun
quiz.explanation: Perihelion, the closest point, falls in early January. That this happens in the northern winter is strong evidence that distance does not cause the seasons.

quiz.q: It is late June. Which of these places has the longest daylight?
quiz.explanation: In late June the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun, and the farther north you go the longer the day. Oslo gets almost 19 hours of daylight; places on the equator get about 12, and Sydney, in winter, gets fewer than 12.

challenge.title: A one-week sky diary: the Moon and a bright planet
challenge.prompt: For seven days in a row, go out at about the same time each evening (or each morning, if the Moon is only up then) and record the Moon and one bright planet. For each entry, write the date, time and place; sketch or describe the Moon’s shape and which side is lit; and note its compass direction and its height in fists. Identify the planet with a free sky chart or NASA’s monthly skywatching guide and note where it is compared with the Moon or a landmark. On cloudy nights, write that it was cloudy. Finish by explaining what changed over the week and why.
challenge.deliverable: Seven dated diary entries (at least four with observations), followed by a paragraph of 100 to 200 words explaining how and why the Moon’s shape and position changed.
rubric: Entries are complete: date, time, place, Moon shape with lit side, direction and height in fists
The recorded phases follow the correct order and match the dates
The explanation uses our changing view of the Moon’s sunlit half, not Earth’s shadow, and mentions the Moon’s eastward drift of about 12 degrees a day
The planet is identified and its position recorded consistently, with a note on how it moved, or did not, against the Moon or the stars

challenge.title: Set a friend straight about the seasons
challenge.prompt: A friend insists that summer happens because Earth gets closer to the Sun. Write a short, friendly explanation that would change their mind. Give at least two pieces of evidence against the distance idea, explain the real cause, and describe a simple demonstration they could do at home with a flashlight or with a lamp and a ball. Use at least two real numbers from this chapter.
challenge.deliverable: A message of 150 to 250 words written to your friend.
rubric: Gives at least two correct pieces of evidence: perihelion in early January, the small 3 percent change in distance, or opposite seasons in the two hemispheres
Explains that the 23.4-degree tilt changes both the Sun’s height (concentration of sunlight) and the length of the day
Describes a home demonstration that actually shows the idea
Uses at least two accurate numbers and plain, friendly language

review.by: Researched and written with web-search verification; then fact-checked independently by a second agent. WebSearch worked and was used to confirm the Foucault Panthéon details (28 kg bob, 67 m wire, about 11.3 degrees per hour at Paris), Foucault's Comptes rendus 32, 135-138 paper (presented 3 February 1851), and Ottewell's Thousand-Yard Model (1989, Universal Workshop; NOIRLab URL eduprog032; 1 inch = 100,000 miles, 8-inch Sun, peppercorn Earth 26 yards away). Direct page fetches failed (NASA, NOIRLab and university hosts could not be reached), so the NASA fact-sheet values were checked from expert knowledge. All numbers were recomputed independently: equator speed, sunlight ratio, pendulum rate, day lengths at 40 degrees N and in Oslo, noon Sun heights, scale-model sizes, and the error of the explorer's declination formula (at most about 1.4 degrees). Every figure's geometry was checked from its SVG coordinates. Every answer key was re-solved blind.

corrections.before: Williams, D. R. (2024, November 15). Earth fact sheet.
corrections.after: Williams, D. R. (n.d.). Earth fact sheet.
corrections.why: The page and its values are real (sidereal rotation 23.9345 h, equatorial radius 6,378.137 km, perihelion 147.1 and aphelion 152.1 million km, obliquity 23.44 degrees), but I could not confirm a 'Last Updated: 15 November 2024' date (the NASA host could not be reached, and searches did not show the footer). Use n.d., as the chapter already does for the Moon fact sheet.

corrections.before: Williams, D. R. (2024, November 15). Earth fact sheet.
corrections.after: Williams, D. R. (n.d.). Earth fact sheet.
corrections.why: Same citation as 1.1 source 2. The update date could not be confirmed, so it should be n.d.

corrections.before: A pendulum keeps swinging in the same direction in space; nothing makes it turn.
corrections.after: Nothing in a pendulum makes its swing turn by itself.
corrections.why: The swing plane stays fixed in space only at the poles. At other latitudes it turns relative to the ground at 15 degrees times sin(latitude) per hour (about 11.3 degrees per hour at Paris, 48.85 degrees north). That is why the next sentences say the rate depends on latitude. Saying the swing keeps one direction in space contradicts that and would confuse a careful beginner.

corrections.before: so the Moon gains a little less height than the full three fists
corrections.after: so the Moon gains only about two fists of height
corrections.why: I worked this out for 40 degrees north. Starting 10 degrees up, 30 degrees of turning along the slanted path raises the Moon to about 31 to 33 degrees: a gain of about 21 to 23 degrees, or two fists, not 'a little less than three'. The step's conclusion, about three fists above the horizon, is correct only because the gain is about two fists.

corrections.before: like a grain of fine sand
corrections.why: In the model the Moon is about 0.55 mm across (3,475 km at 1 inch per 100,000 miles). Fine sand is about 0.125 to 0.25 mm; a 0.5 mm grain is medium to coarse sand.

corrections.before: In the Northern Hemisphere the noon shadow is shortest around the June solstice and longest around the December solstice.
corrections.after: North of the tropics, the noon shadow is shortest around the June solstice and longest around the December solstice.
corrections.why: Between the equator and 23.4 degrees north, the noon shadow is shortest, and vanishes, on the days the Sun passes overhead (spring and late summer), not at the June solstice. On the June solstice the shadow there points south.

corrections.before: The five planets you can see with your eyes alone
corrections.after: The five planets that are easy to see with your eyes alone
corrections.why: Uranus (about magnitude 5.7) can just be seen with the naked eye under very dark skies. The five classical planets are the ones that are easy to see.

corrections.before: This was the first experiment anyone could watch that showed the ground itself turning.
corrections.after: It let anyone watch the ground itself turning.
corrections.why: Earlier falling-body experiments (Guglielmini 1791, Benzenberg 1802, Reich 1831) had already detected Earth's rotation, so 'first' depends on the exact wording and is hard to check. The softened sentence keeps the point without a priority claim.

review.summary: The chapter is accurate. Every key number I recomputed is correct (1,670 km/h, 7 percent, 11 degrees per hour and 32 hours, 73 and 27 degrees, 15 and 9 hours, almost 19 hours in Oslo, 0.5 mm and 6 cm, 24 m), all 14 answer keys are right, and all three figures are geometrically correct, down to the Arctic Circle touching the terminator. The corrections are minor: an unconfirmed fact-sheet date, a pendulum sentence that contradicts the latitude dependence, an overstated height gain in one worked example, and three small over-generalizations.
